conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is supported and not false, citing pivotal phase 3 trial data showing a statistically significant reduction in new vertebral fractures with abaloparatide compared to placebo, as well as systematic review evidence.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false.** The strongest evidence is the placebo-controlled, randomized phase 3 ACTIVE trial in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Over 18 months, abaloparatide reduced *new vertebral fractures* versus placebo; the reported incidences were 0.6% with abaloparatide and 4.2% with placebo (p<0.0001). This is an absolute reduction of about 3.6 percentage points and a relative reduction of about 86%. The trial also found fewer nonvertebral fractures.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf

The result is not based solely on a manufacturer claim: a later systematic review/meta-analysis likewise concluded that abaloparatide has a protective effect and can reduce vertebral-fracture risk in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38307725/

**Important limits:** The evidence directly supports treatment for postmenopausal women with osteoporosis—particularly those at high fracture risk—and the pivotal comparison was for daily injections over 18 months. It does not mean every individual will avoid fracture, establish benefit beyond that study period without subsequent-management evidence, or demonstrate a reduction in hip fractures specifically. The FDA indication is for postmenopausal women at high risk for fracture or who have failed/intolerated other osteoporosis therapies.  
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=712143d9-e21e-4013-bb3b-3426a21060a8&audience=consumer
